      <title>Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/kenyan-doomsday-sect-leader-jailed-murders-paul-mackenzie</link>
      <description><p>Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families</p><p>The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.</p><p>The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/19/kenya-starvation-cult-leader-guilty-murder-190-children">found the cult leader guilty</a> of the crimes.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/kenyan-doomsday-sect-leader-jailed-murders-paul-mackenzie">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/anc-faces-defeat-south-african-local-elections</link>
      <description><p>Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result</p><p>The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.</p><p>Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Fri, 06 Nov 2026 21:57:34 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category>Eye on Africa</category><title>Kenyan cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/kenyan-cult-leader-sentenced-to-200-years-in-prison</link><description>
In tonight's edition, cult leader Paul Mackenzie is sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 190 children starved ‌to death on his orders. Also, in South Africa, activists warn that new data centres could put added pressure on already strained water and electricity supplies. And Senegal continues to celebrate the spirit of sport at the Youth Olympic Games.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/70a84f88-da28-11f1-a6e4-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-1380a6db.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/70a84f88-da28-11f1-a6e4-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-1380a6db.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">60735d84-da27-11f1-b58b-2bb8317d3868</guid><pubDate>Fri, 06 Nov 2026 21:23:53 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Clarisse FORTUNÉ</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Europe bomb hoaxes widen</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/europe-bomb-hoaxes-widen</link><description>
The series of hoax bomb scares sent to several Irish media outlets and European airlines are likely part of a coordinated campaign of disruption, according to the Irish government. Dozens of commercial flights have been targetted by email with threats said to be over and above the typical hoax in specificty. Ireland's broadcaster RTE who's staff evacuated the premises this morning and several Italian airlines, say they received a mesage cliaming to be from a Russian extremist group calling itself the Fighters of the Male State, which denied its implication. France 24's Jean-Emile Jammine speaks to Eric Schouten, founder and CEO of Dyami Security Intelligence.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d4fadc82-da26-11f1-bdcc-d18c5759e759/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-2027abfe.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d4fadc82-da26-11f1-bdcc-d18c5759e759/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-2027abfe.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">1932fd32-da25-11f1-8828-79379f6052bc</guid><pubDate>Fri, 06 Nov 2026 21:22:24 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Americas</category><title>Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay for first stop on 12-day South America tour</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261106-pope-leo-arrives-in-uruguay-for-first-stop-on-12-day-south-america-tour</link><description>
Pope Leo touched down in Uruguay on Friday to begin a 12-day tour of South America that will also see him visit Argentina and Peru. The tour is seen as something of a homecoming for the pontiff who lived in Peru for almost two decades and holds joint US and Peruvian citizenship.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/0aab0508-da1a-11f1-81c8-d18c5759e759/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-06T193927Z-1437835472-RC2JIOACA4EZ-RTRMADP-3-POPE-LATAM-URUGUAY.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/0aab0508-da1a-11f1-81c8-d18c5759e759/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-06T193927Z-1437835472-RC2JIOACA4EZ-RTRMADP-3-POPE-LATAM-URUGUAY.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">3283e0f4-da24-11f1-a6d8-95d5f1845f91</guid><pubDate>Fri, 06 Nov 2026 21:14:49 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/0aab0508-da1a-11f1-81c8-d18c5759e759/w:1024/p:16x9/2026-11-06T193927Z-1437835472-RC2JIOACA4EZ-RTRMADP-3-POPE-LATAM-URUGUAY.jpg">© Yara Nardi, Reuters</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Americas</category><title>Trump announces immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as new chief of staff</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261106-trump-announces-immigration-hardliner-stephen-miller-as-new-chief-of-staff</link><description>
US President Donald Trump on Friday said advisor Stephen Miller would become his new chief of staff. Miller has been instrumental in driving the Trump administration's mass deportation programme and faced particular criticism after the deadly shootings of two Minneapolis protesters by ICE agents in January.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/e4ccbd52-da20-11f1-92bf-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D6PN3T3.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/e4ccbd52-da20-11f1-92bf-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D6PN3T3.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">ac163ece-da21-11f1-a81a-0383cf3d852d</guid><pubDate>Fri, 06 Nov 2026 20:51:37 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/e4ccbd52-da20-11f1-92bf-a575454bc579/w:1024/p:16x9/000-D6PN3T3.jpg">© Chip Somodevilla, AFP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category>The World This Week</category><title>Midterms: A Maga PostMortem, Europe’s ‘Shape Shifting’ Protests</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/the-world-this-week/20261106-midterms-a-maga-postmortem-europe-s-shape-shifting-protests</link><description>
A World This Week ‘Mid Terms Special’ 
 
Gavin Lee is joined by panel of four distinguished international correspondents to assess the aftermath of the worst Republican election result since the 1970s, post Watergate. We ask, is peak MAGA over? What will now change at home and abroad? And who ends the week in pole position as Presidential frontrunner for 2028?

On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day.

Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star."

At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago. Because Tycho's Star is 13,000 light-years from Earth, it took a while before anyone could see it.

Why it mattered

The Tycho supernova, known technically as SN 1572, is known today as a Type Ia supernova, which is a star explosion in a binary star system in which a white dwarf star draws material away from its partner, then explodes. But in 1572, the Tycho supernova appeared as something very different: a bright new star.

While Schulër was first, other astronomers also observed the apparently new star in the sky. Tycho Brahe's numerous observations are the most well known, in no small part becuause he wrote a book all about them in "De Stella Nova" (Latin for "On The New Star." At the time, the prevailing theory among scientists was that the stars were unchanging, yet here was a new star -- a changed sky.

"The 16th century exploding star, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia, was seen in daylight for about two weeks, and remained visible to the naked eye for 16 months," the University of California Berkeley wrote in 2004. "Brahe's meticulous record of the brightening and dimming of the supernova now allows astronomers to identify its 'light signature" as that of a Type Ia supernova."

"This was at the end of the Dark Ages in Europe, and these observations were an important piece of evidence that the heavens were not immutable," astronomer Alex Filippenko, who led a 2004 study on the origins of the Tycho supernova, said at the time.

Today, astronomers are closely watching another star that might explode. Called T Corona Borealis, or the Blaze Star, the object is expected to be on the verge of exploding in a nova (a star explosion that is smaller than a supernova and may not destroy the star). is one of 11 known stars observed to have recurring nova explosions within gaps of 100 years or so.

]]> <![CDATA[ AST SpaceMobile announces new 'Blacklift' rocket, targets 2028 launch debut ]]> Another new private rocket is in the works.

AST SpaceMobile announced today (Nov. 6) that it's building a reusable rocket called Blacklift to launch its broadband satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO), with first flight targeted in 2028.

The news comes just 10 days after Cowboy Space unveiled Big Iron, a rocket designed to launch its constellation of 20,000 AI data centers. Cowboy Space is also targeting 2028 for its first liftoff.

"The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry," Abel Avellan, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, said in a statement today.

"This will accelerate our mission to build a new layer of global connectivity, extending connectivity beyond terrestrial networks and helping to bring AI-enabled services wherever people live, work and travel," Avellan added.

Texas-based AST SpaceMobile is building a LEO constellation composed of its BlueBird satellites, which beam internet service directly to cell phones. The company has launched 13 BlueBirds to date, including eight "Block 2" variants. The antennas on each of these next-gen spacecraft cover a whopping 2,400 square feet (223 square m) — the largest ever deployed in LEO by a commercial satellite.

BlueBirds have flown atop three different rockets to date — SpaceX's Falcon 9, Blue Origin's New Glenn and India's Launch Vehicle Mark-3. But AST SpaceMobile wants to get more vertically integrated, which explains the push to develop Blacklift.

The company won't be starting from scratch. It has signed a deal with another Texas-based outfit, Firefly Aerospace, to provide the engines (and associated engineering services) for the first three Blacklift launches. After that, AST SpaceMobile will build the engines itself, under a licensing agreement with Firefly.

Those engines are Miranda, which will power Blacklift's booster, and Vira, which will power the upper stage.

Neither engine has flight experience. (Firefly's currently operational rocket, Alpha, uses Reavers in its booster and Lightnings in its upper stage.) But Miranda has been tested extensively on the ground, firing for more than 4,200 seconds over the course of 175 hot fires, according to AST SpaceMobile.

"The Miranda engine will allow us to leapfrog the traditional five-to-10-year development cycle as we build Blacklift," AST SpaceMobile President Scott Wisniewski said in the same statement.

The "supply and services" agreement for the first three launches is worth $500 million. The licensing agreement cost AST SpaceMobile about $800 million, with half of that paid in cash and half in stock, according to the statement.

Blacklift will be able to haul 20 tons to LEO. Each launch will therefore be able to loft up to five BlueBird satellites, according to today's announcement. (For perspective: The Falcon 9's LEO lift capacity is about 25 tons.)

BlueBirds will continue going up while AST SpaceMobile gets Blacklift ready to fly: The company already holds contracts with other providers to launch more than 100 of the satellites over the course of 2027 and 2028.

The launch landscape will likely be very different when Blacklift, Big Iron and other new rockets come online. SpaceX has said that it plans to phase out the Falcon 9, as well as its Falcon Heavy heavy lifter, after its Starship megarocket gets up and running.

That milestone could come in the next few years, ushering in something of a launch crunch for satellite operators. SpaceX has indicated that it will prioritize launches of its own satellites with Starship. And there will be a lot of them to loft — 100,000 Starlink V3 satellites and a million Starmind AI data centers, company founder and CEO Elon Musk has suggested.

]]> <![CDATA[ What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all! ]]> Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!"

The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence.

On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky. And the view is only going to get better in the days and weeks to come!

Ascending in the morning

In terms of morning visibility, Venus is now in a literal and figurative sense "rising to the occasion." It's now rising before the break of dawn, more than 90 minutes before sunrise. From here on, it will rise three minutes earlier each day, so that by Dec. 17 it will rise 3 hours and 50 minutes before sunrise and blaze in a completely dark sky for more than two hours before the first vestige of morning twilight.

It will reach peak brilliance on Nov. 29, when it will shine at an eye-popping magnitude of -4.9. That's 12 times brighter than its nearest planetary competitor, Jupiter and a full 25 times more dazzling than Sirius, the brightest of all stars. If you live in a rural location with no light pollution to interfere, you might be able to make out that it is casting a visible shadow and if you follow it right on through sunrise, it will be evident to your naked eye in full daylight: a tiny white speck plainly evident against the blue daytime sky.

In a way, we could even regard Venus as this year's version of a "Christmas Star," glowing with stunning radiance ". . . in the east" like the biblical quote mentioned in St. Matthew.

What goes up, must come down

After reaching its high point in terms of morning visibility in mid-December, Venus will start a long, slow slide back toward the sun, rising about 1½ minutes later each morning from New Year's Day through late March. By then, Venus will be coming up as dawn is breaking, roughly 100 minutes before sunrise. Venus will continue to get gradually lower and rise progressively later during the spring and by late June it will be coming up less than an hour before sunrise, ultimately vanishing into the bright dawn twilight by July. Venus will then go on a "summer sabbatical" of sorts and will not reappear again until about this time next year when it will begin a very fine evening apparition.

So, if any of your friends or relatives remark to you that they saw a "strange UFO" on the way to work or school recently, you now can set them straight.

It's not E.T. It's only Venus.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

]]> <![CDATA[ You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it ]]> The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned.

I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way. Would she like to see it?

She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied.

There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece.

That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target.

What's happening and when to look

Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects.

I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31.

You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle.

I'm going to look for Andromeda this week in the least heroic way possible. No expedition. No mountain-top observing location. No elaborate equipment. I'll wait until it is properly dark, step outside and then use Cassiopeia and the stars of Andromeda to work my way toward M31. I'll then reach for my 10x50 binoculars, which are rarely far from my side after dark, whether I'm at home or traveling. The more light-sensitive parts of the retina away from the center of our vision can make faint objects easier to detect. They crossed intergalactic space for roughly 2.5 million years and ended their trip in your retina. Stargazing is often described as looking back in time. With Andromeda, that phrase stops being a metaphor.

From Alpheratz, follow a curving line of stars away from the square through Mirach and on toward Almach. That gives you the basic shape of Andromeda — not the easiest constellation to imagine as a mythological princess, but a useful chain of stars to learn.

]]> <![CDATA[ Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight ]]> Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star.

The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world.

The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight.

The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight.

"For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement. "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden."

There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight.

The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem.

Telescopes their more stable digital twins

The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors.

This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image.

To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets.

The researchers found that, in terms of detecting faint exoplanets, FLIP outperformed conventional image-processing techniques two to 15 times. This led to ERI b emerging from data collected by the JWST two years ago.

"We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn't see," Wang said. "This is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didn’t have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way."

The team hopes that FLIP can now be adopted by other astronomers in a bid to recover hitherto undiscovered exoplanets that have been hidden by the glare of their stars.

This could be a major boon for NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, which aims to directly photograph Earth-like planets orbiting distant sun-like stars.

"We know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system," team leader Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez of Northwestern University said. "It's not that they don’t exist. It's that we cannot see them.

"Every time we improve our techniques, we discover new types of planets. By finding more planets, we can better understand how planetary systems form and evolve, and ultimately how typical our own solar system truly is."

The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Nature.

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it.

The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system.

"The first thing we said was, 'Wow,'" Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement about the image, which ESA released on Thursday (Nov. 5). "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world."

What is it?

The Didymos system consists of the eponymous 2,560-foot-wide (780 meters) space rock and its "moonlet" Dimorphos, which is about 530 feet (160 m) in diameter.

The DART mission impacted Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, with the aim of causing a change in the orbital period of the moonlet. And it worked: Before the impact, Dimorphos completed one lap around Didymos in around 11 hours and 55 minutes. The DART collision reduced the length of this period by around 33 minutes.

The change is a result of the fact that Dimporphos is now traveling at around 2.7 millimeters per second more slowly than it did before the collision.

The newly released photo shows Didymos in detail. Just a sliver of Dimorphos is visible, below and slightly to the left of the main asteroid.

Why is it incredible?

The changes caused by DART were small. But in a real Earth-threatening scenario, even such a tiny shift could help divert an asteroid on a collision course — as long as scientists get enough advance warning of its approach.

Hera's observations should help reveal what other changes have occurred on and around Didymos.

Scientists are already seeing that, while Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator as before the impact, many changes have occurred. This includes the creation of multiple boulders, craters, and patterns of grooves or ridges.

"Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 kilometer [0.62 miles] of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out," said Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist. "We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

Stay tuned to Space.com for more Hera findings from Didymos.

]]> <![CDATA[ Northern lights could reach New York and Idaho this weekend as speedy solar wind races toward Earth ]]> The northern lights could put on an impressive display this weekend as a colossal coronal hole on the sun fires a stream of high-speed solar wind toward Earth.

Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions between Nov. 6 and Nov. 8, with a chance of moderate (G2) conditions on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC).

If G2 conditions materialize, the northern lights could be visible as far south as New York and Idaho.

What is happening?

The culprit behind the potential uptick in northern lights is a large coronal hole on the sun, a region where the sun's magnetic field opens up. They allow streams of charged particles known as the solar wind to escape more easily into space. Coronal holes appear darker in ultraviolet images because they are cooler and less dense than their surroundings.

And this particularly large — and rather oddly shaped — coronal hole is sending some seriously speedy wind our way.

The U.K. Met Office forecasts solar wind speeds between 342 and 404 miles (550-650 kilometers) per second, considerably faster than the typical speed of around 249 miles (400 km) per second.

The fast solar winds are expected to arrive around Nov. 6-7 and could persist through much of the weekend. It could interact with Earth's magnetic field, potentially triggering geomagnetic storms and fueling spectacular aurora shows. The stronger the storm, the farther south the northern lights can potentially be seen.

Where will auroras be visible?

Under G1 conditions, auroras may be visible from northern Michigan and Maine, but if activity intensifies to G2 levels, skywatchers farther south, including those in New York and Idaho, could be in for a treat.

But remember! Aurora forecasts are notoriously tricky. Much depends on the strength and orientation of the magnetic field carried by the incoming solar wind, particularly whether it points southward, allowing more energy to transfer to Earth's magnetic field.

Northern Hemisphere aurora forecast courtesy of the U.K. Met Office

To give yourself the best chance of seeing the northern lights, keep an eye on those aurora forecasts, head somewhere dark away from city lights if you can, with a view of the northern horizon.

To stay updated on space weather and know the best times and places to catch auroras, consider using a space weather app tailored to your location. One app I recommend is "My Aurora Forecast & Alerts," available on both iOS and Android. Another great tool is the "Space Weather Live" app on iOS and Android, which offers more in-depth insights into current space weather conditions and their potential for aurora activity.

Pomohou zachraňovat životy</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/zdravi/905055-vyrazene-sanitky-z-libereckeho-kraje-miri-na-ukrajinu-pomohou-zachranovat-zivoty.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/zdravi/905055-vyrazene-sanitky-z-libereckeho-kraje-miri-na-ukrajinu-pomohou-zachranovat-zivoty.html</guid><pubDate>Fri, 06 Nov 2026 11:03:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Zdraví</category><description>Další tři sanitky, které dosud sloužily záchranářům v Libereckém kraji, zamíří na Ukrajinu. Ve středu 4. listopadu 2026 se ve sportovní hale ve Varnsdorfu uskutečnilo okresní kolo florbalového turnaje ČEPS Cupu, určeného pro žáky 1.–5. tříd základních škol.

Turnaj se hrál systémem 3 + 1. Každý tým se utkal s každým soupeřem dvoukolově, přičemž jedno utkání trvalo 2 × 8 minut. Na turnaji se představily tři týmy – ZŠ Východní, Centrum dětí a mládeže Česká Kamenice a naše škola. Každý tým tak odehrál celkem čtyři utkání. Vítězný tým turnaje postoupí do krajského finále.

Hned v úvodním utkání nás čekal nejtěžší soupeř, domácí ZŠ Východní. Po velmi vyrovnaném a bojovném průběhu jsme dokázali zvítězit těsným výsledkem 4:3. Druhý zápas proti soupeři z České Kamenice jsme zvládli výborně a po přesvědčivém výkonu jsme zvítězili 6:2. Ve druhém kole jsme se znovu utkali se ZŠ Východní. Tentokrát nám soupeř porážku oplatil a po dramatickém průběhu jsme prohráli nejtěsnějším rozdílem 2:3. Jelikož i ZŠ Východní zvítězila nad Českou Kamenicí, bylo před závěrečným utkáním jasné, že o vítězi turnaje rozhodne počet vstřelených branek proti tomuto soupeři.

Do závěrečného utkání jsme proto nastoupili s jasnou taktikou – vstřelit co nejvíce branek. Po většinu turnaje nás v brance skvěle držel Adam Reichert, který několika výbornými zákroky podržel tým v nejtěžších chvílích. Pro rozhodující utkání jsme však zvolili odvážný taktický tah. Adama jsme přesunuli z branky do pole, protože sehraná trojice Adam Reichert, Hugo Bláha a Dominik Košín měla za úkol nastřílet co nejvíce gólů. Tento plán dokonale vyšel. Našemu týmu se podařilo zvítězit vysokým rozdílem a vstřelit soupeři 13 branek, tedy o tři více, než dokázala ZŠ Východní. Díky lepšímu skóre jsme se stali vítězi okresního kola a vybojovali si zasloužený postup do krajského finále.

Velkou pochvalu si zaslouží celý tým za bojovnost, nasazení a kolektivní výkon. V našem týmu nastoupila také jediná dívka Barča Šeráková, která byla velmi platnou hráčkou a svým výkonem významně přispěla k celkovému úspěchu. Z individuálních výkonů bych chtěla vyzdvihnout Huga Bláhu, Adama Reicherta, Maxe Zachariáše a Dominika Košína, kteří patřili k oporám našeho týmu. Poděkování však patří všem hráčům za výbornou reprezentaci školy.
